clues.text: In Eden, he gave names to all the livestock, the birds of the air, and every beast of the field.
In Eden, the LORD God made a woman from a rib taken from him and brought her to him.
After he ate from the forbidden tree, God told him the ground was cursed and he would toil.
In the earliest record of generations, he lived a total of 930 years and then died.
God drove him out of Eden and placed cherubim with a flaming sword to guard the tree of life.
Writing to Corinth, Paul says that as in him all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.
Luke traces the family line of Jesus back through Seth to him, the son of God.
Eve's younger son, he was a keeper of sheep while his older brother worked the soil.
He brought the LORD the best portions of the firstborn of his flock, and God looked on him with favor.
A son of Adam, he was invited by his brother to go out to the field and was killed there.
A New Testament roll of the faithful says he was commended as righteous and by faith still speaks though dead.
The sprinkled blood of Jesus, mediator of a new covenant, speaks a better word than his blood.
Soon after Eden, God said the voice of this son's blood was crying out to Him from the ground.
Jesus warned the scribes and Pharisees about the righteous blood shed on earth, from his blood to Zechariah's.
After Jesus and his disciples sang a hymn at the Last Supper, they went out to a mount named for this fruit.
When the trees sought a king in Jotham's story, this tree refused, unwilling to stop giving its oil.
In a vision, Zechariah saw two of these trees beside a solid gold lampstand, one on each side.
Paul told Gentile believers they were a wild shoot grafted into this tree to share its nourishing root.
A psalm of blessing says the sons of a man who fears the LORD will be like these shoots around his table.
Samson's foxes, with torches tied to their tails, burned the Philistines' grain, vineyards and groves of these trees.
In the temple's inner sanctuary, Solomon made two cherubim, each ten cubits high, from this tree's wood.
A relative of Abram, he went along when Abram obeyed the LORD and left Haran for the land of Canaan.
After his herdsmen quarreled with Abram's herdsmen, he chose the well-watered plain of the Jordan for himself.
Four kings carried him off from Sodom, and Abram chased them with 318 trained men to rescue him.
Sitting in the gateway of Sodom, he welcomed two angels into his house and baked them unleavened bread.
Told by angels to flee Sodom to the mountains, he begged to escape to a small nearby town instead.
His two daughters bore sons named Moab and Ben-ammi, fathers of the Moabites and the Ammonites.
Peter calls him a righteous man, tormented by the lawless deeds he saw while living in Sodom.
Early one morning, Jacob set up the stone from under his head as a pillar here and poured oil on it.
At the altar in this city, King Jeroboam stretched out his hand against a man of God, and it withered.
As Elisha walked up the road to this city, a group of boys came out and jeered at him as a baldhead.
Amaziah, the priest of this place, sent word to King Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him.
Abram pitched his tent with this town to the west and Ai to the east, and built an altar there.
King Josiah pulled down Jeroboam's altar in this city, burned the high place, and ground it to powder.
During the war against Benjamin, all Israel went up here, wept before the LORD, and fasted until evening.
At a well near Haran, Jacob rolled the stone away and watered the sheep this shepherdess brought.
Jacob served Laban seven years for her, and it seemed but a few days because of his love.
After Jacob's wedding feast, Laban gave him her older sister Leah instead, and Jacob found out in the morning.
After years without children, Jacob's wife named her first son Joseph and asked the LORD for another son.
When Laban searched the tents, she hid his household idols in her camel's saddlebag and sat on them.
With her last breath, she named her newborn son Ben-oni, but Jacob called the boy Benjamin.
After Herod killed the boys of Bethlehem, a voice was heard in Ramah: she was weeping for her children.
Leah named this son after saying, "This time I will praise the LORD," and then she stopped having children.
When his brothers planned to kill Joseph, this brother asked what profit they would gain from covering up his blood.
Told that his daughter-in-law Tamar was pregnant, this son of Jacob ordered her brought out and burned to death.
After Saul died, the men of this tribe came to Hebron and anointed David king over their house.
When the LORD in His anger removed Israel from His presence, only this tribe remained.
Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah were young men from this land, chosen to serve the king of Babylon.
Jacob said the scepter would not depart from this son, nor the staff from between his feet.
After God called them a stiff-necked people, the Israelites stripped off their jewelry from this mountain onward.
When the thirsty Israelites grumbled, God told Moses to strike the rock at this place so water would pour out.
Strengthened by bread and water from an angel, Elijah walked forty days and forty nights to reach this mountain of God.
A psalm recalls that at this place the Israelites made a calf and worshiped a molten image.
Moses reminded Israel that here God spoke to them out of the fire, and they saw no form at all.
Moses noted that it was an eleven-day journey from this place to Kadesh-barnea by way of Mount Seir.
When Solomon's priests set the ark in the temple, it held only the two stone tablets Moses placed in it here.
As the people waited for Moses to come down the mountain, this leader told them to bring him their gold earrings.
Among twelve tribal staffs left in the Tent of the Testimony, his staff for Levi sprouted, blossomed, and produced almonds.
When the LORD's anger burned against Moses, He named this brother who could speak well and was coming to meet him.
As Joshua fought the Amalekites, he and Hur held up Moses' tired hands until sunset.
His sons Nadab and Abihu put incense in their censers and offered unauthorized fire before the LORD.
On Mount Hor his priestly garments were put on his son Eleazar, and he died there.
When a plague broke out after Korah's rebellion, he ran among the people with incense and made atonement.
He told Balak's servants that not even a house full of silver and gold could make him defy the LORD.
The angel of the LORD stood in his road with a drawn sword, and his donkey turned off into a field.
The king of Moab sent messengers to summon him from Pethor, by the Euphrates in the land of his people.
Before seeking the LORD, he told the king of Moab to build seven altars and prepare seven bulls and seven rams.
Hired to curse Israel, he blessed them three times, and the king of Moab struck his hands together in anger.
He foretold that a star will come forth from Jacob and a scepter will arise from Israel to crush Moab.
On the road to Moab, the LORD opened his donkey's mouth, and she asked why he had beaten her three times.
He commanded the army of Jabin king of Canaan and lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.
Told that Barak had gone up Mount Tabor, he called out nine hundred iron chariots to the River Kishon.
When the LORD routed his army before Barak, he abandoned his chariot and fled on foot.
As he lay sleeping from exhaustion, the wife of Heber the Kenite drove a tent peg through his temple.
Hiding in Jael's tent, he told her to answer 'No' if anyone asked whether a man was there.
His mother peered through the lattice, asking why his chariot was so long in coming.
In the song of Deborah and Barak, the stars fought against him from their courses.
After the victory over Sisera's army, he and Deborah the prophetess sang a song together.
Called to fight Sisera, he said he would go only if Deborah the prophetess went with him.
Deborah warned this commander the honor would not be his, because the LORD would hand Sisera to a woman.
He chased Sisera's chariots and army to Harosheth-hagoyim, and not a single enemy soldier was left.
Arriving in pursuit of Sisera, he was led into Jael's tent and found the enemy commander dead.
Speaking to Israel, Samuel said the LORD sent him, along with Jerubbaal and Jephthah, to rescue them from enemies.
In a list of the heroes of faith, he is named right after Gideon and just before Samson.
King David bought Araunah's threshing floor to build this, so the plague on the people would stop.
Abraham arranged wood on this, then bound his son Isaac and laid him on top.
With stones, Elijah built this in the name of the LORD and dug a trench around it.
Afraid of King Solomon, Adonijah ran and took hold of its horns.
In Isaiah's vision, a seraph flew to him with a glowing coal taken from this with tongs.
Jesus taught: leave your gift in front of this, and first go make peace with your brother.
In Athens, Paul found one of these with the inscription TO AN UNKNOWN GOD.
Grieving for his people, Jeremiah asked if there was no balm here and no physician.
Jacob fled from Laban toward these hills, and Laban chased him seven days to catch him there.
Gideon told every fearful soldier to turn back and leave this mount, and twenty-two thousand went home.
The Reubenites and Gadites, who had very large herds, saw this land was good for livestock.
Its men held the Jordan fords and made fleeing Ephraimites try to say Shibboleth.
Elijah the Tishbite, who told King Ahab there would be no dew or rain, came from among its settlers.
In the Song of Solomon, the bride's hair is like a flock of goats streaming down its mountain.
In the Valley of Sorek, a woman lulled him to sleep on her lap and had his seven braids shaved off.
Near the vineyards of Timnah, the Spirit of the LORD came on him and he tore apart a roaring young lion.
At Lehi the ropes fell from his arms, and he struck down a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone.
Bracing against two central pillars, he pushed with all his might and brought a Philistine temple down on its lords.
He tied torches between the tails of three hundred foxes and burned the Philistines' standing grain.
At midnight in Gaza, he pulled up the city gate, doors and posts, and carried it to a mountain overlooking Hebron.
During a seven-day feast, he bet thirty linen garments on a riddle about something sweet coming out of the strong.
Abraham weighed out four hundred of these in silver to Ephron the Hittite to buy a burial place for Sarah.
Elisha foretold that at Samaria's gate, a seah of fine flour would sell for just one of these.
While hunting lost donkeys, Saul's servant offered a quarter of one in silver to pay the man of God.
When Israel's men were counted in a census, rich and poor alike paid half of one to atone for their lives.
Moses collected five of these for each firstborn Israelite beyond the number of the Levites, to redeem them.
Joseph's brothers pulled him out of the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty of these in silver.
Amos condemned merchants who wanted to shrink the ephah, make this bigger, and cheat with dishonest scales.
When Mary and Joseph brought the baby Jesus to the temple, Simeon told Mary one would pierce her soul.
In a prison holding Paul and Silas, the jailer woke, saw the doors open, and drew one to kill himself.
After felling Goliath with a stone, David pulled the giant's own from its sheath and cut off his head.
While rebuilding the wall of Jerusalem after the exile, each builder worked with one strapped at his side.
Paul told believers to take the helmet of salvation and the one of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
Ehud made a double-edged one a cubit long and strapped it to his right thigh under his cloak.
When Jesus was arrested, Simon Peter drew one and cut off the right ear of Malchus, the high priest's servant.
Naboth owned a vineyard in this place, right next to the palace of King Ahab.
When Jehu arrived in this city, Jezebel painted her eyes, adorned her head, and looked down from a window.
As heavy rain fell, Elijah tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way here.
Before Gideon blew the ram's horn, the Midianites and Amalekites crossed the Jordan and camped in this valley.
While the Philistines gathered their forces at Aphek, Israel's army camped by the spring at this place.
Wounded by the Arameans at Ramah, King Joram son of Ahab came back to this city to recover.
The seventy sons of King Ahab were slaughtered, and their heads were sent in baskets to Jehu at this place.
Elijah the Tishbite told this king of Israel there would be neither dew nor rain except at his word.
In the third year of drought, this king of Israel met Elijah and called him the troubler of Israel.
This king of Israel married the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and then served Baal.
This king lay on his bed, face turned away, refusing to eat because a Jezreelite would not sell his vineyard.
After Aram's defeat, this king of Israel took Ben-hadad into his chariot and released him by a treaty.
When Elijah pronounced doom on his house, this king tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and fasted.
After this king of Israel died in battle, dogs licked his blood when his chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria.
In Aram, a young girl captured from Israel told her mistress a prophet in Samaria could cure her master's leprosy.
Elisha sent a messenger to tell this leper from Aram to wash himself seven times in the Jordan.
Angry at the prophet's word, he asked if Abanah and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, were not better than Israel's waters.
Healed at the Jordan, this Aramean went back to Elisha and declared there is no God in all the earth except in Israel.
When Elisha refused his gift, this Aramean asked to be given as much soil as a pair of mules could carry.
He commanded the army of the king of Aram and was highly regarded and valiant, but he was a leper.
Jesus told a synagogue crowd that of all Israel's lepers in Elisha's time, only this Syrian was cleansed.
A messenger told Daniel the prince of this kingdom opposed him twenty-one days, until Michael came to help.
Nebuchadnezzar's captives served him and his sons in Babylon until this kingdom came to power.
In Daniel's vision, the two-horned ram stood for the kings of Media and this land.
At Susa, Vashti's banishment was written into the laws of Media and this land, so it could never be repealed.
Ezekiel said men of this land, along with Lydia and Put, served as warriors in the army of Tyre.
The Jerusalem temple was finished under decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, all kings of this land.
Daniel was told three more kings would arise here, then a richer fourth who would stir everyone against Greece.
In his first year, this king of Persia proclaimed that God's people could go up and rebuild the temple in Jerusalem.
This king had his treasurer Mithredath count out the temple articles Nebuchadnezzar took and hand them to Sheshbazzar.
Through Isaiah, the LORD called this ruler His shepherd who would fulfill all He desired, and said Jerusalem would be rebuilt.
Through Isaiah, God called this foreign king His anointed, whose right hand He grasped to subdue nations.
When Darius ordered a search, a scroll in Ecbatana showed this king had decreed the temple's costs be paid from the royal treasury.
After God rescued Daniel from the lions, Daniel prospered during the reigns of Darius and this Persian king.
Zerubbabel turned down enemies who offered to help build the temple, saying this Persian king commanded Israel alone to build it.
At the king's gate in Susa, he would not bow down or pay homage to Haman.
In Susa, he brought up his orphaned cousin Hadassah and took her as his own daughter.
Sitting at the king's gate, he learned two eunuchs were plotting to kill King Xerxes and reported it.
Haman had a gallows fifty cubits high built to hang him, but Haman was hanged on it instead.
Haman was ordered to dress him in a royal robe and parade him on the king's horse through Susa.
When Haman's decree to destroy the Jews went out, he tore his clothes and wailed in sackcloth and ashes in Susa.
King Xerxes gave him the royal signet ring that had been taken back from Haman.
When Mordecai would not bow down or pay him homage, he was filled with rage.
He offered King Xerxes ten thousand talents of silver for the royal treasury to pay those who carried out a decree of destruction.
In the days of King Xerxes, the Pur, that is the lot, was cast before him to choose a day and month.
His wife Zeresh and his friends told him to build a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai.
He robed Mordecai and paraded him on a horse through the city square as the man the king delights to honor.
The Jews in the citadel of Susa killed five hundred men, including this man's ten sons.
In Susa, he was hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai, and the king's fury subsided.
Joseph, a Levite the apostles called Barnabas, came from here and sold a field for the church.
Sent out by the Holy Spirit, Barnabas and Saul sailed here from Seleucia and preached in Salamis synagogues.
Ezekiel pictured Tyre as a ship whose deck was made from wood of this land's coasts, inlaid with ivory.
After a sharp disagreement with Paul, Barnabas took Mark and sailed off to this place.
Men from here and Cyrene went to Antioch and began telling Greeks the good news about Jesus.
Sailing toward Italy as a prisoner, Paul's ship passed in the lee of this island because of contrary winds.
Balaam's oracle said ships would come from the coasts of this land and subdue Asshur and Eber.
Coming before the LORD among the sons of God, he asked the LORD whether Job feared God for nothing.
When Peter rebuked Jesus for foretelling His death, Jesus called Peter a stumbling block and addressed him by this name.
He rose up against Israel and stirred King David to take a census of the people.
For forty days in the wilderness he tempted Jesus, who was there among the wild animals.
Peter asked Ananias why he had let this one fill his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit about the land money.
As the chief priests looked for a way to kill Jesus before Passover, he entered Judas Iscariot.
When the seventy-two returned rejoicing over the demons, Jesus said He saw him fall like lightning from heaven.
On a road outside the city, the prophet Ahijah tore his new cloak into twelve pieces and told this man to take ten.
So his people would not go up to Jerusalem, this king of Israel made two golden calves and set them in Bethel and Dan.
In battle against King Abijah of Judah, this king of Israel sent troops behind them in ambush, but God routed him.
When King Solomon sought to kill him, this man fled to Shishak king of Egypt and stayed until Solomon died.
This king sent his wife in disguise to the old, blind prophet Ahijah to ask about their sick son.
Seeing this young Ephraimite servant was industrious, Solomon put him over the labor force of the house of Joseph.
This king of Israel built shrines on the high places and appointed priests from every class of people who were not Levites.
Lot looked out and saw the Jordan plain was well watered, like the garden of the LORD and like this land.
During the great famine, ten of Joseph's brothers traveled down to this land to buy grain.
When Moses stretched out his hand toward heaven, total darkness covered all of this land for three days.
An angel told Joseph in a dream to take the Child and His mother and flee here from Herod.
Mocking King Hezekiah, the Assyrian envoy called this land a splintered reed that pierces the hand leaning on it.
Complaining in the wilderness, Israel remembered the fish, cucumbers, melons and leeks they ate freely here.
The Israelites lived in this land for 430 years before the LORD's divisions went out of it.
In a parable of Jesus, one of these men saw a man beaten by robbers and passed by on the other side.
In the wilderness, the LORD took these men for Himself in place of every firstborn son of Israel.
Whenever Israel's camp moved in the wilderness, these men took down the tabernacle and set it up again.
They received no land among Israel's tribes; the LORD gave them Israel's tithes as their inheritance instead.
When Israel settled the land, these men were given forty-eight cities to live in, with pasturelands around them.
King David declared that no one but these men could carry the ark of God, since the LORD chose them.
Leaders from Jerusalem sent priests and these men to John the Baptist to ask him, "Who are you?"
Abram moved his tent to live near the Oaks of Mamre in this town and built an altar there.
Abraham buried his wife Sarah in the cave of the field at Machpelah, near this town in Canaan.
The spies Moses sent went up through the Negev to this town, where descendants of Anak lived.
Joshua blessed Caleb son of Jephunneh and gave him this town as his inheritance.
In the hill country of Judah, this town was a city of refuge for the manslayer.
King David reigned over Judah from this city for seven years and six months before ruling in Jerusalem.
Absalom asked King David to let him go to this town to fulfill a vow to the LORD.
King Omri bought this hill from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city on it.
Before His ascension, Jesus told the apostles they would be His witnesses in Jerusalem, all Judea, and here.
Elisha led a blinded Aramean army into this city, then prayed for their eyes to be opened.
Naaman's young Israelite servant girl said a prophet in this city could cure her master's leprosy.
The king of Assyria besieged this city for three years, captured it, and exiled the Israelites.
On His way from Judea to Galilee, Jesus had to pass through here and stopped at Jacob's well.
Philip preached Christ in a city here, where Simon the sorcerer had long amazed the people.
In the days of the judges, a Bethlehem man fled a famine with his wife and two sons to live here.
Lot's older daughter gave her son this name, and he became the father of a whole people.
Balak son of Zippor, king of this land, sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel.
The LORD buried Moses in a valley in this land, and no one knows where his grave is.
Ehud, a left-handed Benjamite, was sent with tribute to Eglon, the king of this land.
While hiding from danger, David asked this land's king to let his father and mother stay with him.
Its king Mesha was a sheep breeder who gave Israel's king a hundred thousand lambs.
Moses fled from Pharaoh to this land and sat down beside a well.
Moses' father-in-law Jethro served as the priest of this land.
God told Gideon He would deliver this people into his hand with only the three hundred men who lapped water.
The men of Ephraim captured Oreb and Zeeb, two princes of this people, and brought their heads to Gideon.
In a war Moses sent with Phinehas, Israel killed five kings of this people, and Balaam too.
Elders of this people went with Moab's elders to Balaam, carrying fees for divination and Balak's message.
Traders from this people sold young Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, captain of Pharaoh's guard.
After Moses stretched out his staff over Egypt, an east wind blew all night and brought them by morning.
When Pharaoh begged for mercy, a strong west wind swept them into the Red Sea.
Through the prophet Joel, God promised to repay His people for the years eaten by these.
In Gideon's day the Midianites invaded Israel with their camels and tents like a great swarm of these.
Among four small but wise things on earth, these have no king yet all advance in formation.
When the fifth angel sounded his trumpet, these came out of the smoke from the Abyss with power like scorpions.
In a vision, the prophet Amos saw these eat every green plant, and he begged God to forgive.
King David told Nathan the prophet he lived in a house of this while the ark of God stayed in a tent.
Exiles back from captivity paid men of Sidon and Tyre to bring logs of this from Lebanon to Joppa by sea.
Solomon paneled the temple's inner walls with this wood, carved with gourds and flowers, so no stone could be seen.
In King Solomon's day, Jerusalem had this as plentiful as sycamore trees in the foothills.
To cleanse someone healed of a skin disease, the priest used two birds, scarlet yarn, hyssop, and this wood.
Hiram king of Tyre sent David logs of this wood, along with carpenters and stonemasons, to build his palace.
King Jehoash of Israel told of a thistle in Lebanon asking this tree to give its daughter in marriage.
Reuben found mandrakes in the field during the wheat season of this, and Rachel begged Leah for them.
Naomi and Ruth arrived in Bethlehem from Moab just as the barley season of this began.
Solomon told the slacker to learn from the ant, which gathers its food at the time of this.
Joseph advised Pharaoh to take a fifth of this in Egypt during the seven years of abundance.
Moved with compassion for the crowds, Jesus told His disciples this is plentiful but the workers are few.
God told Israel that when gathering this, they must leave the field's edges and gleanings for the poor.
In the parable of the weeds, Jesus said this stands for the end of the age.
God told Aaron to lay both hands on a live one, confess Israel's sins over it, and have a man send it into the wilderness.
Joseph's brothers slaughtered one and dipped his robe in its blood before sending the robe to Jacob.
In a vision beside the Ulai Canal, one charged a two-horned ram and shattered both its horns.
In Jesus' parable, the older son complained that his father never gave him a young one to celebrate.
Gideon set a young one and unleavened bread on a rock, and fire flared up when the angel's staff touched them.
Rebekah put the skins of young ones on Jacob's hands and neck so Isaac would take him for Esau.
Jacob asked Laban for every speckled or spotted one of these, along with the dark lambs, as his wages.
